newsitem.title: UK: Abandoned car held explosives, Northern Irish police say.
newsitem.headline: Abandoned car held explosives, Northern Irish police say.

text.p: A car believed to have been abandoned by maverick Irish republican guerrillas in Belfast contained homemade explosives and bomb components, Northern Irish police said on Monday.

Police destroyed the vehicle in a controlled explosion in the bomb first incident since the Irish Republican Army declared a truce at the end of August, 1994, in its campaign to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
The IRA called off its truce in February and has since planted several bombs on the British mainland and in Germany, but it has not carried out any attacks in Northern Ireland.

"The vehicle was found to contain a large plastic bag...a quantity of granular material was found, together with an alarm clock, batteries and electrical wiring," a police spokeswoman said. "At this stage it is believed it was a bomb."
Police said the car contained about 250 pounds (110 kg) of homemade explosives. Security sources were unable to say whether it had been primed to explode.
The incident coincided with a the resumption of multi-party peace talks between majority Protestant pro-British parties and minority Catholic Irish politicians on Monday.
Sinn Fein, the IRA's politial wing, is barred from the talks because the guerrilla group has refused to call off hostilities.
The car used in the latest incident was hijacked in a Roman Catholic district of Belfast by three masked men and left in a public square.
A warning was telephoned late on Sunday to a newspaper by a man claiming to represent the "Irish Continuity Army", a maverick republican group opposed to British rule over Northern Ireland.
The shadowy group was blamed for an attack on a hotel in Enniskillen, 75 miles (120 km) west of Belfast, in July. It is composed of a small group of hardliners who opposed the IRA ceasefire.
